package_info.package_manager: Windows Executable (PE file, distributed via ZIP archive)
package_info.why_malicious: The package is a Windows executable that masquerades as a document by using double extensions (e.g., .pdf.exe, .xls.exe) and document icons. Upon execution, it harvests sensitive system, hardware, and user information and exfiltrates it to attacker-controlled command-and-control (C2) servers using hardcoded endpoints. The executable performs no legitimate user-facing function and is solely intended for unauthorized data collection, reconnaissance, and exfiltration, representing a clear infostealer threat.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, upon user execution of the disguised .exe file
execution_context.file_location: Dropped executable (e.g., 'CMK Правила оформления больничных листов.pdf.exe')

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon user execution of the disguised executable, the code collects basic system and user information (OS type, host name, user name), computes a unique client hash, and sends this data to a remote C2 server via HTTP POST with a custom cookie header, resulting in initial victim identification and data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code collects system and user identifiers and immediately exfiltrates them to a hardcoded external server using a custom HTTP header, which is a common infostealer tactic for victim fingerprinting.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate document or application would not collect and transmit system or user data to an unknown server, especially not immediately upon execution and without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise asset management tools may inventory system info, but only with user or administrator awareness and transmission to trusted, internal endpoints.
key_indicators: Immediate data exfiltration to hardcoded C2 domain
Custom identifier in HTTP cookie header (3rd_eye=<hash>)
Execution triggered by user opening a disguised executable

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Harvesting detailed hardware and user data and sending it to an external, hardcoded server is not expected for any legitimate document or utility, and is indicative of reconnaissance and data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not enumerate hardware, user accounts, or desktop files and transmit them externally without explicit user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System inventory tools may collect such data, but only with explicit user or administrator consent and transmission to trusted, internal infrastructure.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting such a broad set of system, network, and software information and sending it to an external server is highly indicative of reconnaissance for further attacks and is not justified by any legitimate document functionality.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software, especially when disguised as a document, does not perform extensive enumeration of system and network state and exfiltrate this data externally.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise management agents may collect similar data, but only with user or administrator consent and transmission to trusted, internal endpoints.

Inventory of installed and user programs
Outbound HTTP POST to hardcoded C2 domain

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, upon user execution of the disguised .exe file

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon user execution of the disguised executable, the code encodes all collected system and user data in hexadecimal format and exfiltrates it to the C2 server via HTTP POST, increasing the difficulty of detection and analysis.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Encoding exfiltrated data in hexadecimal is a common anti-analysis and evasion technique in malware, intended to bypass simple content inspection and hinder forensic analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not obfuscate or encode telemetry data before sending it to unknown or untrusted servers, especially when the data includes sensitive system and user information.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate telemetry may be encoded for protocol reasons, but only when sent to trusted, internal endpoints and with user awareness.
key_indicators: Outbound HTTP POST to hardcoded C2 domain

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, upon user execution of the disguised .exe file

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon user execution of the disguised executable, the code exfiltrates collected data to an internal IP address via HTTP POST, likely for testing, staging, or evasion of external network monitoring.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of internal IP addresses for C2 communication is highly unusual for legitimate software and suggests either testing, staging, or attempts to evade detection by avoiding external network traffic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not send sensitive data to arbitrary internal IPs without explicit user or administrator configuration and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Internal telemetry may be sent to known, trusted infrastructure in enterprise environments, but only with proper configuration and user awareness.
key_indicators: C2 communication to internal IP addresses (e.g., 10.10.30.36, 192.168.21.182)

attack_chain.action: User is lured into opening a ZIP archive containing a file with a double extension (e.g., .pdf.exe or .xls.exe), disguised as a document with a document icon and Russian-language filename.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the malicious infostealer executable

attack_chain.action: Malicious executable runs and collects system, user, hardware, and network information from the victim's machine using multiple data collection routines.
attack_chain.leads_to: Preparation of collected data for exfiltration

attack_chain.action: Collected data is optionally encoded (e.g., hexadecimal) for obfuscation prior to transmission.
Data is exfiltrated to a hardcoded C2 server or, in some variants, to an internal IP address for testing or evasion.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives victim data for reconnaissance, profiling, or future attacks

behavioral_signatures: Execution of files with double extensions (e.g., .pdf.exe, .xls.exe) masquerading as documents and using document icons
Enumeration of system, hardware, user, and network information immediately after execution of the dropped executable
Outbound HTTP POST requests to hardcoded C2 domains or internal IPs with collected system data in the request body
Use of custom HTTP headers (e.g., Cookie: 3rd_eye=<hash>) for victim identification during exfiltration
Encoding (e.g., hexadecimal) of exfiltrated data prior to transmission to C2 endpoints
file_indicators: Files with double extensions (e.g., .pdf.exe, .xls.exe) in user download or temporary directories
Dropped executables with Russian-language filenames (e.g., 'Табель учета рабочего времени.xls.exe', 'CMK Правила оформления больничных листов.pdf.exe')
Presence of executables with document icons masquerading as legitimate documents
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to domains: shlalala.ru, ohmycars.ru, anime-clab.ru, glovatickets.ru (all using /ch3ckState or /general/ch3ckState endpoints)
HTTP POST requests to internal IPs (e.g., 10.10.30.36, 192.168.21.182) on /ch3ckState endpoint
Custom HTTP header: Cookie: 3rd_eye=<hash> used in outbound requests
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of files with double extensions and document icons, especially those originating from ZIP archives and with Russian-language filenames. Detect processes that enumerate system, hardware, and user information immediately after launch. Inspect outbound HTTP POST requests to known C2 domains (shlalala.ru, ohmycars.ru, anime-clab.ru, glovatickets.ru) or internal IPs, particularly those containing system inventory data or using custom headers like '3rd_eye'. Flag exfiltration attempts where data is encoded (e.g., hexadecimal) prior to transmission. Correlate these behaviors to identify infostealer activity and prevent unauthorized data exfiltration.
